'''Jacob Cohen''' (April 20, 1923 – January 20, 1998)<ref name=jama></ref> was an American [[psychologist]] and [[statistician]] best known for his work on [[statistical power]] and [[effect size]], which helped to lay foundations for current statistical [[meta-analysis]]<ref name=Saxon></ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://media.wiley.com/product_data/excerpt/04/04708608/0470860804-2.pdf |title=Cohen's entry in Encyclopedia of Statistics in Behavioral Science |access-date=2008-02-15 |archive-date=2016-01-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160130075524/http://media.wiley.com/product_data/excerpt/04/04708608/0470860804-2.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=jama>{{Citation|title=Jacob Cohen, PhD, 1923-1998 |journal=Archives of General Psychiatry |year=1999 |volume=56 |first=Michael |last=Borenstein |url=http://archpsyc.ama-assn.org/cgi/content/extract/56/6/581 |doi=10.1001/archpsyc.56.6.581 |page=581 |issue=6 |pmid=23538686 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070808075641/http://archpsyc.ama-assn.org/cgi/content/extract/56/6/581 |archivedate=August 8, 2007 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and the methods of [[estimation statistics]]. He gave his name to such measures as [[Cohen's kappa]], [[Cohen's d|Cohen's ''d'']], and [[Cohen's h|Cohen's ''h'']].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781118445112 |title=Wiley StatsRef: Statistics Reference Online |date=2014-09-29 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-1-118-44511-2 |editor-last=Kenett |editor-first=Ron S. |edition=1 |language=en |doi=10.1002/9781118445112.stat06274 |editor-last2=Longford |editor-first2=Nicholas T. |editor-last3=Piegorsch |editor-first3=Walter W. |editor-last4=Ruggeri |editor-first4=Fabrizio}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/0470013192 |title=Encyclopedia of Statistics in Behavioral Science |date=2005-04-15 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-470-86080-9 |editor-last=Everitt |editor-first=Brian S. |edition=1 |language=en |doi=10.1002/0470013192.bsa109 |editor-last2=Howell |editor-first2=David C.}}</ref>

== Education and career ==

Cohen grew up in a Yiddish-speaking household and learned English at school. He attended the [[Townsend Harris High School]] and graduated at the age of 15. He entered the [[City College of New York]], where he first studied mathematics but was interrupted by a service in the [[US Army intelligence]] during [[World War II]] in Europe.<ref name=ampsych></ref> He eventually received a BA in psychology in 1947 from the City College.<ref name=Saxon></ref> He then obtained his Master's degree in 1948 and PhD in clinical psychology at [[New York University]] (NYU) in 1950. His PhD advisor was Avrum Ben-Avi.<ref name=thesis>{{Cite web |last=Cohen |first=Jacob |date=1950 |title=A comparative analysis of the factors underlying intelligence test performance of different neuropsychiatric groups |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/301832256}}</ref> Cohen worked in the hospitals affiliated with the [[Veterans Administration]] after graduation, first at Bronx, then at Montrose VA Medical Center, where he was a director of research.<ref name=ampsych></ref> Between 1959 and retirement in 1993, he worked in the psychology department at NYU, latterly as the head of the [[quantitative psychology]] group.<ref name=Saxon>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/02/07/nyregion/jacob-cohen-74-psychologist-and-pioneer-in-statistical-studies.html|title=Jacob Cohen, 74, Psychologist and Pioneer in Statistical Studies|newspaper=The New York Times|date=7 February 1998|last1=Saxon|first1=Wolfgang|access-date=16 February 2017|archive-date=10 January 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110210559/http://www.nytimes.com/1998/02/07/nyregion/jacob-cohen-74-psychologist-and-pioneer-in-statistical-studies.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1969 Cohen married Patricia Ruth Childs (1936-2018), later Patricia Cohen, who was a former PhD student in psychology at NYU.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Patricia Cohen, Who Tracked Mental Health of Children, Dies at 81 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/07/31/obituaries/patricia-cohen-who-tracked-mental-health-of-children-dies-at-81.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180731233306/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/07/31/obituaries/patricia-cohen-who-tracked-mental-health-of-children-dies-at-81.html |archive-date=2018-07-31 |language=en}}</ref>

After retirement from NYU, Cohen continued working as a statistical consultant at the [[Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center]], [[New York State Psychiatric Institute]], and at their joint H.I.V. Center for Clinical and Behavioral Studies. Cohen passed away in 1998 at the [[St. Vincent's Hospital and Medical Center]] in New York City.<ref name=Saxon></ref>

Cohen was president of the [[Society of Multivariate Experimental Psychology]] in 1969. He was awarded the Distinguished Lifetime Achievement Award by the [[American Psychological Association]] in 1997 and was a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], the American Psychological Association and the [[American Statistical Association]].<ref name=Saxon></ref>

== Power analysis and significance testing ==
In addition to being an advocate of power analysis and effect size, Cohen was a critic of reliance on, and lack of understanding of, [[significance testing]] procedures used in statistics, especially misunderstandings of [[null hypothesis]] significance testing.<ref>{{Cite web |first=Joachim I. |last=Krueger |title=What Cohen meant |url=https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/one-among-many/201104/what-cohen-meant |website=Psychology Today |language=en-US}}</ref> In particular, he identified the "near universal misinterpretation of p as the probability that H<sub>0</sub> is false, the misinterpretation that its complement is the probability of successful replication, and the mistaken assumption that if one rejects H<sub>0</sub> one thereby affirms the theory that led to the test".<ref>Cohen, J. (1994). The earth is round (''p'' < .05). ''American Psychologist, 49''(12), 997–1003. doi:10.1037/0003-066x.49.12.997</ref> He encouraged instead a recognition of single studies as exploratory and a reliance on [[Replication (statistics)|replication]] for support.
Cohen developed known interpretation thresholds for the correlation ''r'' and the standardized mean difference ''d''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Holmes |first=Alexander |last2=Illowsky |first2=Barbara |last3=Dean |first3=Susan |date=2023-12-13 |title=10.2 Cohen's Standards for Small, Medium, and Large Effect Sizes - Introductory Business Statistics 2e {{!}} OpenStax |url=https://openstax.org/books/introductory-business-statistics-2e/pages/10-2-cohens-standards-for-small-medium-and-large-effect-sizes |website=openstax.org |language=English}}</ref>
